content.p: Giuseppe Piromalli, known to investigators and the press as "Facciazza," has been at the centre of one of Calabria's most powerful 'ndrangheta families. He was born in 1945. He was a fugitive for six years, was arrested in a fortified hideout in Gioia Tauro in March 1999, served 22 years under Italy's 41-bis prison regime, and was released in 2021. Four years later he was among 26 people arrested in an investigation prosecutors called Res Tauro. He is an accused man in that case. Reports do not give a verdict, and they do not record how he has pleaded.
content.h2: A clan built around the Gioia Tauro plain
content.p: The Piromalli family controlled the plain around Gioia Tauro, a town in southern Calabria. La Stampa describes the clan as already established in the postwar decades. Its criminal power grew as large public works reached the area, including a new steelworks and the Salerno to Reggio Calabria motorway. According to La Stampa, companies working on the port and the steel plant were asked in 1974 for a payment of 3 per cent to be left alone. The clan's leaders refused and demanded subcontracts instead, and so took more than half of the subcontract work, the paper reports.

The family's leader was Giuseppe's uncle, Mommo Piromalli. He died of natural causes in 1979, and another uncle, Giuseppe "Peppino" Piromalli, took over. Peppino Piromalli died in prison in 2003. Accounts differ on what happened next. Quotidiano Nazionale says Pino Piromalli succeeded his uncle at the head of the clan. Il Fatto Quotidiano reports that prosecutors believe he led the clan with his brothers until 1999, and continued to direct it while he was in detention.

The port of Gioia Tauro, by La Stampa's account, became the largest commercial port in the Mediterranean. In 1994 a terminal company, Medcenter Container, was set up with 128 billion lire of state financing, and a shipping group, Contship, leased part of the port. La Stampa says the Piromalli clan pressed both companies into paying a dollar and a half for every container handled, which it describes as half of the profit the two companies made on each one. Quotidiano Nazionale describes the same arrangement as a 50 per cent cut of the profit on each container.

Il Fatto Quotidiano quotes a 1996 conversation in which a clan member, Domenico Pepé, tells a senior figure at the terminal company that the clan asks a dollar and a half a container. The same paper says the port was long regarded as a gateway for cocaine from South America, and that the Piromalli family was one of several in the Gioia Tauro plain whose members had links to businesses working inside the port.

The Guardian reported in 1999 that two of the charges against Piromalli concerned alleged efforts to extort kickbacks and to control the award of contracts by the port's management. It also reported that he was accused of trying to extract 100,000 pounds a year from the television network of Silvio Berlusconi, in return for not blowing up its relay stations in Calabria. Those were allegations at the time of his arrest, and reports do not show how they were decided.
content.h2: The fugitive years and the 1999 arrest
content.p: Piromalli had been on the run since 1993, when he was placed on a list of the most dangerous fugitives in Italy. The Independent called him one of Italy's 30 most wanted criminals. The arrest came in March 1999, and the sources give slightly different dates. Il Fatto Quotidiano says he was found on 10 March. The Independent and The Guardian, both dated 12 March, say the arrest happened the day before.

Police tracked him to a derelict-looking house in Gioia Tauro. The Guardian reported that inside was a comfortable two-storey residence, with a large store of champagne, and that the carabinieri needed pneumatic drills to get through the security doors. The Guardian described about 70 armed carabinieri surrounding the building and said it seemed Piromalli made no attempt to escape. La Stampa says he was unarmed and did not resist arrest, and that the hideout contained an altar with images of the Madonna di Polsi, a shrine in the Aspromonte mountains.

Italy's prime minister, Massimo D'Alema, called the arrest an important success, according to The Guardian. The head of the parliamentary anti-mafia commission, Ottaviano Del Turco, said the hideout was the tenth found in Calabria with sophisticated equipment, and that the authorities needed to find the workshops that had built it. The Guardian said it was highly likely that an informer had alerted the carabinieri to the hideout, but it did not name one.

Piromalli's court record is mixed. At first instance he was given a life sentence for the 1998 murder of Luigi Ioculano, a doctor active in local politics in Gioia Tauro. On appeal he was acquitted for insufficient evidence, and Il Fatto Quotidiano reports that Italy's highest court upheld that acquittal. The same paper says he was convicted of mafia association and extortion, and of an association aimed at winning public contracts for port works, and that he served time for those convictions.

In December 2020 he was acquitted in the "Provvidenza" trial, according to Il Fatto Quotidiano, which describes it as his most recent acquittal before his release. Reports do not give the full charges or the reasoning in that trial.

His son Antonio was arrested in July 2008 in the "Cento anni di storia" operation, according to Quotidiano Nazionale. Il Fatto Quotidiano says he had a final conviction in that case, and reports that Antonio was arrested again in January 2017 in Operation Provvidenza, in which prosecutors ordered the detention of 33 people accused of mafia association and drug trafficking, among other charges. The paper says Antonio controlled Milan's fruit and vegetable market.

After 22 years under the 41-bis regime, which restricts prisoners' contact with the outside world, Piromalli was freed in May 2021. Il Fatto Quotidiano reports that he finished his sentence at the prison in Viterbo and returned to Gioia Tauro, where he was given three years of supervised freedom. Quotidiano Nazionale gives the release date as 11 May 2021, while a court document quoted by the same paper gives 10 May. The reports do not settle which date is correct.

Il Fatto Quotidiano describes the return as a homecoming to the territory that had been his uncles' domain. Quotidiano Nazionale, quoting the judge's order in the Res Tauro case, says that after his release he set about rebuilding the clan's authority. That is an allegation in an investigation, not a finding of any court.

On 23 September 2025, carabinieri from the Ros special operations group, with provincial units, carried out a custody order issued by a judge in Reggio Calabria at the request of the Reggio Calabria district anti-mafia office. Quotidiano Nazionale reports that 26 people were arrested in eight Italian cities, from the north to the south of the country. Among them was Giuseppe Piromalli, then 80. Open notes that the name evokes Gioia Tauro, the clan's historic domain.

The suspects were accused, according to the same reports, of mafia-type association, extortion, money laundering, self-laundering, illegal possession of weapons and ammunition, bid-rigging, aiding a suspect and fraudulent transfer of assets. The charges were aggravated by the use of mafia methods. Six of the 26 were already in prison for other offences. Investigators said the seizures included property worth about 3 million euros, and that more than 4 million euros were frozen in accounts linked to Piromalli and to a close associate, Antonio Zito.

The judge's order, as quoted by Quotidiano Nazionale, describes Piromalli as the central figure in the clan's leadership. It says he redefined the roles of members after his release, reasserted control of the territory through extortion of businesses, and interfered with court-ordered property auctions so that the clan could recover seized assets or take contracts. Open reports an intercepted conversation in which Piromalli describes himself as the boss of Gioia. Investigators, as Open and La Stampa report them, say his aim was to restore the old 'ndrangheta rules inside the clan.
These are the allegations of the investigators and the judge, not findings of a court. Reports do not record a plea, a trial date or any ruling on the evidence.
content.h2: Earlier property seizures and a 2008 vote-fraud claim
content.p: A police press release dated 30 June 2009 reported the seizure of property worth about 10 million euros in Gioia Tauro and Milan, as a follow-up to the Cento anni di storia operation. The release linked the assets to the Piromalli family, and it described an apartment block in Gioia Tauro that had belonged to the family.

In 2008 The Guardian reported that Corriere della Sera had linked an Italian senator and aide to Silvio Berlusconi, Marcello Dell'Utri, to an alleged plan to add 50,000 fraudulent votes to the overseas ballot. Italian newspapers said investigators believed a businessman, Aldo Micciché, was working with members of the Piromalli clan on the plan. Micciché denied the allegations, and Dell'Utri described the reports of his own links to the scheme as "lies and garbage." Reports do not show that Giuseppe Piromalli was charged in that matter.
content.h2: What the record still leaves open
content.p: Several points are unsettled in the reports. The first is the exact date of his 1999 arrest, which is given as 10 March by one paper and as the day before 12 March by two others. The second is his release date in May 2021, where a court document and a newspaper differ by a day. The third is the outcome of the 1991 killings of Antonio and Michele Versace, for which The Guardian said in 1999 that he faced trial; reports do not give a result. The fourth is the family relationship of Antonio Piromalli. Most reports call him Giuseppe's son, but a 2009 police release calls him a nephew.

The most important open question is the Res Tauro case itself. The charges are on the record, and the judge's order sets out the investigators' account, but no verdict has been reported. Until a court rules, the allegations against Giuseppe Piromalli remain allegations, and his name is linked to the crimes described only in the way the investigators and newspapers report them.
